title: Why did Mars become a desert?
subtitle: From rivers to desert
subject: sciences
description: More than 3 billion years ago, rivers carved valleys and floods swept across the surface of Mars. Today the planet is cold and dry, but its water has not all disappeared.
author: muhammad-zaheer

hero.hook: Rivers, deltas, lakes: the red planet was not always a frozen desert.

blocks.text: For decades, scientists have searched Mars for signs of past life. All known life needs water, yet the Martian surface today is cold and extremely dry. Mars was not always like this, though: rovers, the wheeled robots that explore its ground, have found rocks and minerals that only form in the presence of **liquid water**.

Seen from above, the landscape confirms it: ancient river valleys, deltas, dried-up lakebeds. Many of these features are more than **3 billion years** old. NASA has even found traces of gigantic floods about **3.5 billion years** ago. So water once flowed on Mars. The mystery remains: how did a wet planet turn into this desert?

Having water is not enough. A planet needs conditions that keep it liquid. Today the atmosphere of Mars is very thin: its [[atmospheric pressure]] is less than **1%** of Earth's. Under such low pressure, liquid water does not stay stable on the surface: it freezes or evaporates.

blocks.caption: The fossil delta of Jezero Crater seen from orbit: the sediments of a river in an ancient lake.

blocks.text: So how did early Mars hold on to its water? Billions of years ago, its atmosphere was much thicker, and that helped in two ways. Higher pressure kept water in its liquid state. And the gases in the air trapped heat, a [[greenhouse effect]] that kept the surface warmer.
Scientists still debate exactly how warm early Mars was. One thing is certain, though: liquid water stayed on its surface long enough to carve valleys and fill lakes.

Over billions of years, a large part of that atmosphere escaped into space. The first reason is the planet's size. Mars is small, its **gravity** is weaker than Earth's, and it holds on to its gases less firmly. The second reason: Mars lost its [[magnetic field]], the invisible shield that protected its atmosphere from charged particles from the Sun.

blocks.caption: A NASA visualization (MAVEN mission): the solar wind strips gases from the upper Martian atmosphere.

blocks.text: Those particles form the [[solar wind]], a continuous stream of charged matter flowing out of the Sun. With no shield, it strikes the upper Martian atmosphere and knocks gases away. The most energetic sunlight matters too: it breaks apart water and other molecules, and the **light atoms** released escape the weak gravity of Mars more easily. As the atmosphere thinned, Mars grew colder and drier.

Yet not all of the water on Mars fled into space. Some of it, rising into the upper atmosphere, was indeed broken into light atoms that escaped. But the rest stayed behind: part of it froze beneath the surface, another part reacted with the rocks and ended up locked inside **minerals**.

A study published in 2021 in the journal *Science* estimates that between **30 and 99%** of the water on Mars may have been trapped in the minerals of its rocks. A wide range: the question remains open.

So this water did not simply collect underground as ice or liquid. It is now part of the [[crust]], the planet's outer rocky layer. In other words, a large share of the "missing" water of Mars may still be there, held prisoner in its rocks.

Mars looks like a desert today, but it is not without water. What has largely disappeared is the stable water that once flowed across the surface. Large amounts remain frozen in the [[polar ice caps]], more lies beneath the ground as **buried ice**, and still more is locked inside the minerals of the crust.

blocks.caption: The north polar ice cap of Mars in summer: a spiral of ice on the ocher ground.

blocks.text: The lesson reaches beyond Mars. Having water is not enough to make a planet wet and livable: the conditions matter just as much. A thick enough atmosphere keeps water liquid and lets it gather into rivers and lakes. Mars did not become a desert because every drop flew off into space, but because its atmosphere could no longer keep its water moving.
Mars dried out because its thinned atmosphere could no longer keep liquid water on the surface: much of that water is still there, frozen at the poles or locked inside the rocks.
